title: Senate Advances Bill That Would Reshape College Sports
summary:
The U.S. Senate took a major step this week toward passing a bill that would radically change college sports. Senators voted 74-24 to close debate on the Protect College Sports Act, bringing it closer to a final vote. If it passes the Senate, it goes to the House of Representatives.

The bill would put into law the revenue sharing negotiated under the House settlement, which allows schools to share up to 22% of certain revenue with athletes. This year, that amounts to $21.58 million per school. It also adds a $27.5 million "retention pool" to keep current players on the roster, which could reduce third-party name, image, and likeness (NIL) payments — deals where athletes are paid for their fame.

The legislation offers the NCAA, the governing body for college sports, some protection against lawsuits, especially over eligibility issues. Recently, lawsuits have come from players who graduated high school in 2022 and were denied a fifth year of eligibility under a new rule for the Class of '23. The bill would also preempt state laws that conflict with national guidelines — though exactly how that plays out could be subject to litigation.

Other provisions: athletes would generally be limited to one "free" transfer without sitting out a season, a move that could reduce chaos in the transfer portal. Coaches would be prohibited from leaving one school for another during the season. A rewrite of a 1961 law would let athletic conferences pool their media rights to generate more revenue — but the powerful Southeastern and Big Ten conferences have resisted, saying it wouldn't make more money. The bill would require most schools to maintain the same number of Olympic-sport programs as in 2024-25 for at least nine years. It would provide federal funding for broadband and media infrastructure at historically Black colleges and universities. It would also prohibit conferences from expanding beyond 19 teams and add measures to prevent a breakaway "superleague."
why_it_matters: This bill decides who controls the billions generated by college sports — athletes, universities, or Congress — and it sets the template for how young people are paid for their talent well before they turn professional.

background_read: The NCAA, the National Collegiate Athletic Association, is the non-profit body that writes the rulebook for most U.S. college sports and, until recently, banned athletes from earning money for their fame.
That changed in 2021, when the Supreme Court's NCAA v. Alston decision and new state laws pushed the NCAA to allow name, image, and likeness (NIL) deals, letting players sign sponsorship contracts.

The bill builds on the House settlement, a legal case brought by former athletes seeking back pay for the use of their NIL, which produced a framework letting schools share revenue directly with players. Congress is involved because the NCAA says a patchwork of different state NIL laws makes one national rulebook impossible — and a federal law could also shield it from lawsuits.
The Senate has 100 members, and most bills need 60 votes to overcome a filibuster, which is why the 74-24 vote to cut off debate signals unusually broad support.

Historically Black colleges and universities (HBCUs) often have smaller athletics budgets and less media exposure, so the broadband and infrastructure funding in the bill is aimed at narrowing that gap.

perspectives.description: For the first time, revenue sharing with players would be written into federal law rather than left to courts and patchwork state rules, and the retention pool gives schools a legal way to keep rosters stable. Programs in the wealthiest conferences stand to gain the most from the new money and from protection against lawsuits.

perspectives.perspective: Critical — NIL businesses, some players, and sceptical conferences
perspectives.description: Third-party NIL deals could shrink if money is redirected into the retention pool, and athletes may end up with less freedom to negotiate. The Southeastern and Big Ten conferences oppose the media-rights pooling, arguing it would not generate more money, while state lawmakers may object to federal rules overriding their own NIL laws.

This is the latest step in a decade-long dismantling of amateurism: courts, state legislatures, and now Congress have each chipped away at the NCAA's authority. A federal law could finally give the association the single national standard it has asked for — but at the cost of Congress writing rules it used to control itself.

The bill still needs to pass the House, and its most contested parts — preempting state laws and capping conference size — are likely to end up in court. If it fails, schools and athletes continue under a shifting mix of state laws and settlements, which is exactly the uncertainty Congress is trying to end.
